name: Achilles Tendinopathy
summary: Load-related pain and impaired function in the midportion or insertional Achilles tendon, commonly aggravated by running and hopping.

looksLike: Local tendon pain and morning stiffness
Pain during running, hopping or calf raises
redFlags: Sudden pop and loss of plantar-flexion function (rupture)
Marked sudden loss of plantarflexion strength
firstSteps: Adjust running/jumping load while maintaining tolerable activity
Begin calf isometrics or controlled raises
For insertional symptoms, initially limit deep dorsiflexion compression
selfCare: Continue tolerable tendon loading rather than complete rest
Use footwear modifications only when they clearly improve tolerance

assess: Pain with repeated heel raises or hopping

tests.name: Single-Leg Heel-Raise Test
tests.purpose: Assess calf capacity and symptom response under functional tendon loading.
tests.positive: Familiar Achilles pain, reduced height or lower repetitions compared with other side.

stages.label: Protection, Education & Symptom-Guided Loading
stages.goal: Address safety, settle excessive irritability and maintain useful movement.
do: Adjust running/jumping load while maintaining tolerable activity
Begin calf isometrics or controlled raises
For insertional symptoms, initially limit deep dorsiflexion compression
dose: Heel raises within tolerable range: 3 x 8–12
moveOn: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.

stages.label: Mobility, Strength & Capacity
stages.goal: Restore the specific strength, mobility and control required by the condition.
when: Daily function is stable or improving.
No new red flags or progressive neurological deficit.
Exercise response returns to baseline by the following day.
do: Progress heavy slow calf strengthening with straight and bent knee
Add low-level hopping when strength and pain response allow
dose: Standing and seated calf raises: 3–4 x 6–12, 2–3 days/week
moveOn: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.

stages.label: Functional Restoration & Return to Activity
stages.goal: Rebuild real-world, occupational or sporting capacity.
when: Target movement and resistance are tolerated with good quality.
Functional capacity is improving without sustained symptom flare.
Progression is based on objective performance and patient goals.
do: Progress plyometrics, running speed, hills and sport demands
Increase one load variable at a time
dose: Run-walk progression; increase duration before speed/hills
moveOn: Full task exposure is completed progressively.
No clinically meaningful deterioration during the following 24 hours.

returnCriteria: Repeated single-leg heel raises with adequate height/endurance
Running and sport exposure completed without significant next-day worsening

logic: The tendon usually needs progressive loading, not prolonged rest.
Differentiate insertional from mid-portion pain because deep dorsiflexion may irritate insertional disease.
Monitor total tendon load from walking, running, jumping and exercise.
structures: Midportion Achilles tendon 2–6 cm proximal to insertion or insertional tendon
mechanism: Rapid increase in running, hills or jumping
Reduced calf capacity and recovery mismatch
classification: Insertional tendinopathy; compression sensitivity at end-range dorsiflexion may require modified loading
investigations: Usually clinical; ultrasound/MRI for uncertain diagnosis, suspected tear or atypical course.
Urgent medical assessment for suspected rupture or DVT.
manual: Manual therapy may address ankle mobility restrictions but is not a tendon-healing treatment.
Avoid aggressive friction or stretching that increases insertional compression.
Ankle mobilization if dorsiflexion restriction is clinically relevant
Manual therapy is optional and secondary.
Use ankle mobilization only if a meaningful dorsiflexion restriction limits function.
Soft-tissue work should be brief and should not replace progressive loading.
modalities: Heel lift may temporarily reduce tendon load in selected cases.
Do not use passive modalities as a substitute for progressive calf loading.
Cold or heat for comfort according to preference
Routine therapeutic ultrasound is not essential
dosing: Isometric calf raise hold: 30–45 seconds × 4–5 repetitions when helpful for pain.
Heavy slow calf raises: 3–4 sets × 6–12 reps, 2–4 days/week, progressing load.
Later pogo/hopping and running progression once strength/load tolerance improves.
progression: Progress double-leg → single-leg → heavy → elastic/plyometric loading
Progress load when exercise pain is acceptable and the tendon returns to baseline by the next day.
Add plyometric work before full-speed running.
mistakes: Deep heel drops for irritable insertional tendinopathy
Repeated stretching into painful insertional compression.
Doing only eccentric exercise when other progressive resistance options are suitable.
pearls: Progressive tendon loading is first-line care.
Insertional and midportion presentations may need different starting ranges.
education: Explain that tendon pain can improve with appropriate loading even if some discomfort occurs during exercise.
Use next-day response to judge dose.
Set expectations that recovery may take weeks to months.
escalation: Medical review for suspected rupture, severe insertional pathology or persistent symptoms despite an adequate loading program

tests.name: Single-Leg Heel-Raise Test
tests.purpose: Assess calf capacity and symptom response under functional tendon loading.
tests.positive: Familiar Achilles pain, reduced height or lower repetitions compared with other side.
tests.patientPosition: Stand on one leg with fingertip support; perform controlled full-range heel raises to fatigue or quality limit.
tests.therapistPosition: Position yourself to observe and stabilise the relevant segment without forcing the movement.
tests.handPlacement: Use comfortable, controlled contact appropriate to the test; avoid painful compression or excessive force.
procedure: Explain the test and obtain consent.
Screen contraindications and compare sides when appropriate.
Perform the movement slowly and apply only the required resistance or stress.
Record familiar symptom reproduction, range, strength and side-to-side difference.
tests.interpretation: Quantifies function but does not alone distinguish tendinopathy from partial tear or other causes.
tests.clinicalNote: A special test modifies clinical probability; it does not confirm a diagnosis in isolation.
